Effects of Empagliflozin on Cardiovascular Outcomes Are Consistent Across Sociodemographic Subgroups: A Real-World Analysis From the EMPRISE Study

Cromer SJ, Tesfaye H, Cho H et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Retrospective cohort study (propensity score-matched, real-world claims data analysis)
Key Question: Does empagliflozin's cardiovascular benefit in older adults with type 2 diabetes vary by sociodemographic factors or baseline cardiovascular disease status?
Key Findings:
  • Versus DPP4is, empagliflozin reduced MACE (HR 0.77, 99.9% CI 0.69–0.85), HHF (HR 0.72, 0.67–0.79), and ACM (HR 0.66, 0.57–0.76); versus GLP-1RAs, HHF was reduced (HR 0.88, 0.81–0.95).
  • Absolute risk reductions (IRDs) were consistently larger in patients with prevalent CVD, though relative risk (HR) heterogeneity by CVD status was seen only for HHF.
  • No effect modification by age, sex, race/ethnicity, or socioeconomic status, though a numeric trend favoured greater absolute benefit in those ≥75 years.
Clinical Relevance: Supports equitable SGLT2 inhibitor benefit across diverse elderly NHS patient populations, reinforcing prioritisation in those with existing cardiovascular disease for greatest absolute risk reduction.
Limitations: Observational design using Medicare claims (US, ≥65 years) limits causal inference and generalisability to younger or non-US populations.

Diabetes care

Association of Age at Type 1 Diabetes Onset With Survival, Cardiovascular, and Kidney Outcomes: A Nationwide Cohort Study

Rawshani A, Eliasson B, McGuire DK et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Retrospective nationwide cohort study
Key Question: Does age at type 1 diabetes diagnosis influence long-term mortality, cardiovascular, and kidney outcomes?
Key Findings:
  • Each 1-year older age at diagnosis was associated with 1.7% lower all-cause mortality risk (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.98–0.99), equating to ~8.2% lower risk per 5-year increase.
  • Cardiovascular mortality showed a stronger inverse association (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.97–0.98) than non-cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.98–0.99).
  • Excess risk versus the general population was highest for diagnosis at age 0–10 years, with HRs of 3.23 (all-cause mortality), 5.73 (cardiovascular mortality), and 3.01 (non-cardiovascular mortality).
Clinical Relevance: Reinforces the need for intensive, early cardiometabolic risk surveillance and aggressive management in paediatric-onset type 1 diabetes within NHS paediatric-to-adult transition pathways, given disproportionately high long-term cardiovascular mortality risk in this group.
Limitations: Observational Swedish registry data limit causal inference and generalisability to UK populations with differing diabetes care models.

Diabetes care

An International Position Statement on Practical Approaches for Inpatient Continuous Glucose Monitoring, Insulin Pumps, and Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in Adults

Olsen MT, Spanakis EK, Thabit H et al. · 2026 Sep 22
Study Type: International position statement / expert consensus guideline (not original research).
Key Question: How should CGM, insulin pumps, and automated insulin delivery (AID) systems be practically and safely used in non-critically ill hospitalised adults with diabetes?
Key Findings:
  • Provides selection criteria for continuing or initiating diabetes technology use during admission, including non-critical care settings.
  • Defines CGM-derived glycaemic metrics/targets, alarm thresholds for hypo-/hyperglycaemia, and insulin titration guidance for pump/AID users.
  • Addresses practical workflow issues: perioperative management, imaging-related device considerations, EHR data integration, staff training, and discharge planning.
Clinical Relevance: Offers UK endocrinology teams a structured framework to standardise inpatient diabetes technology use, supporting NHS efforts (e.g., Joint British Diabetes Societies guidance) to reduce inpatient hypoglycaemia/hyperglycaemia and safely manage the growing number of patients admitted with pumps/AID/CGM.
Limitations: As a consensus statement rather than primary data, recommendations rely on expert opinion and existing evidence base rather than new controlled outcome data.

Diabetes care

Automated Insulin Delivery for Pregnancy With Type 1 Diabetes: A Call to Action

T1D Pregnancy & Me Study Group* · 2026 Sep 24
Study Type: Commentary/call to action (non-systematic, position statement)
Key Question: Should automated insulin delivery (AID) systems be adapted and studied specifically for use in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes (T1D)?
Key Findings:
  • Current FDA-approved AID systems are largely not labelled or designed for pregnancy, and most reduce insulin delivery when CGM values fall within ranges considered optimal for fetal well-being, conflicting with tighter pregnancy glycemic targets.
  • Pregnant women have been systematically excluded from AID clinical trials, leaving minimal evidence to guide device use in this population despite AID being standard of care for non-pregnant adults with T1D.
Clinical Relevance: UK endocrinologists managing pregnant women with T1D should recognise that existing AID algorithms may be poorly suited to pregnancy targets, informing counselling, off-label use decisions, and advocacy for inclusion in trials and NHS-led real-world evaluations.
Limitations: As a commentary, it presents no original data or systematic evidence review, relying on expert opinion and identified evidence gaps.

Diabetes care

Predictors of Peak Body Weight Loss With Semaglutide in the SELECT Trial

Lingvay I, Kushner RF, Kaul U et al. · 2026 Sep 24
Study Type: Prespecified secondary analysis of a randomised controlled trial (SELECT)
Key Question: Can routinely available baseline clinical characteristics predict the magnitude of peak weight loss achieved with long-term semaglutide use?
Key Findings:
  • Among 7,594 participants treated ≥1 year, median peak weight loss was 12.5% (IQR 7.9–17.9%), reached at a median of 19 months.
  • The full predictive model explained <10% of variability in peak weight loss; female sex alone accounted for ~8% (85% of the model's explanatory power).
  • Higher maximum dose was associated with greater weight loss (6.0% at 0.24 mg vs 13.3% at 2.4 mg); women on the highest dose achieved the greatest response (16.6% vs 12.4% in men).
Clinical Relevance: For UK clinicians prescribing semaglutide within NHS obesity/cardiometabolic pathways, individual weight-loss response cannot be reliably forecast from baseline characteristics, reinforcing the need for dose titration to maximum tolerated dose and ongoing monitoring rather than pre-treatment risk stratification.
Limitations: The model's low explanatory power suggests unmeasured biological, behavioural, or genetic factors drive treatment response, limiting clinical applicability of the predictors examined.

Diabetologia

Harmine selectively enhances human beta cell identity markers and function via protein kinase A pathways

Wang P, Kumar K, Lambertini L et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Basic/translational laboratory study (human pancreatic islet experiments)
Key Question: Does harmine's ability to enhance beta cell identity and function occur solely through DYRK1A inhibition, or via a distinct second target?
Key Findings:
  • All tested DYRK1A inhibitors (harmine, 2-2c, 5-IT, INDY, leucettine, CC-401, GNF4877) induced beta cell proliferation via DYRK1A inhibition, but DYRK1A gene silencing did not affect identity markers, showing proliferation and identity effects are mechanistically separate.
  • Only harmine, 2-2c and 5-IT enhanced beta cell identity/phenotypic markers (e.g., PDX1, MAFA, NKX6.1), acting through activation of a novel, as-yet unidentified "Target 2" that engages the PKA pathway.
  • This PKA-mediated effect is independent of DYRK1A inhibition, indicating not all DYRK1A inhibitors are functionally equivalent.
Clinical Relevance: For NHS-based regenerative beta cell therapy research in diabetes, these findings highlight that future drug selection/development should prioritise agents combining proliferative and functional-maturation effects, rather than assuming class-wide equivalence among DYRK1A inhibitors.
Limitations: Findings are based on in vitro human islet studies with an unidentified molecular target, limiting immediate clinical translatability.

Diabetologia

Temporal dynamics of daily diabetes-specific burdens using intensive longitudinal data: the central role of feelings of guilt within a multilevel network analysis

Ehrmann D, Hermanns N, Schmitt A et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Pooled analysis of three prospective observational studies using ecological momentary assessment and multilevel network modelling.
Key Question: How do daily diabetes-specific emotional burdens interact and accumulate over time to influence subsequent emotional well-being in type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
Key Findings:
  • In type 1 diabetes, guilt about self-management predicted next-day increases in loneliness (β=0.09), feeling overwhelmed (β=0.05), restricted (β=0.05), and hyperglycaemia burden (β=0.05, all p<0.05); in type 2 diabetes, guilt was instead predicted by prior loneliness and hypoglycaemia burden.
  • Greater overall network density (stronger day-to-day burden interconnection) predicted incident elevated diabetes distress (OR 1.50) and depressive symptoms (OR 2.08, p<0.001), with guilt and feeling restricted as key drivers.
Clinical Relevance: Identifies guilt around self-management as a modifiable, central emotional trigger that could be targeted in structured diabetes education and psychological support pathways within NHS diabetes services to prevent escalation to distress or depression.
Limitations: Observational design with self-report EMA data limits causal inference despite temporal modelling.

Diabetologia

Shared non-HLA genetic architecture across diverse ancestries links insulin secretion and resistance to type 1 diabetes

Fu Q, Wang K, Shen M et al. · 2026 Sep 22
Study Type: Genome-wide association study meta-analysis with integrated functional/epigenetic characterisation
Key Question: Does non-HLA genetic risk for type 1 diabetes overlap mechanistically with genetic determinants of insulin secretion and insulin resistance?
Key Findings:
  • Meta-analysis (26,198 cases, 36,733 controls) identified 69 non-HLA risk loci, including three novel signals (AHI1, TRAF1, ADCY7 regions; ORs 1.07–1.09)
  • 26/69 variants associated with insulin secretion or resistance indices; fine-mapping prioritised 136 functional variants enriched in pancreatic islet, liver, muscle and adipose regulatory elements
  • ADCY7 (16q12.1 locus) identified as a probable causal gene: cytokine exposure downregulated Adcy7 in beta cells, affecting insulin secretion and apoptosis, while adipocyte knockdown improved insulin sensitivity
Clinical Relevance: Suggests type 1 diabetes pathogenesis involves shared genetic pathways with metabolic dysfunction (beyond autoimmunity alone), relevant to UK precision-medicine efforts (e.g., MODY/T1D reclassification, biomarker refinement) and future risk stratification or therapeutic targeting.
Limitations: Findings are largely computational/functional-genomic with limited in vivo human validation, so causal clinical relevance remains preliminary.
